common_name: Guatemalan Blue Banana Squash (Slate-Blue Elongated Heirloom Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil has warmed after last frost; give vines a lot of open ground or a sturdy trellis since fruits can run two feet or more.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has thoroughly warmed, since this Guatemalan heirloom needs a long, hot growing season to fill out its elongated, club-shaped fruit. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so allow generous room or train them up a strong trellis to keep the two-to-three-foot fruits off wet ground. The thin, slate-blue to gray-blue rind hides deep orange, dense, sweet flesh that is excellent baked, and well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot. Cure harvested squash in a warm location for one to two weeks before moving to long-term storage to firm the rind and concentrate sweetness.

planting.note: Direct sow in mid- to late summer, roughly three months before the first fall frost, for a sweet, storable fall and winter crop.

directions: Sow seed directly and thin to a final spacing of six to eight inches, since this Central European heirloom needs room for its globe-shaped root to bulk up. Wilhelmsburger produces a purple-topped, pale yellow-fleshed root known for dense texture and a mild, almost nutty sweetness that intensifies after a light frost. Leave roots in the ground into cool fall weather before harvesting for the best flavor and longest storage life, and use the tender young tops as cooked greens if thinning early plantings.

common_name: Tender and True Parsnip (English Heirloom Smooth-Skinned Parsnip)

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as soil can be worked in spring; parsnip seed loses viability fast, so buy new seed each year.

directions: Sow seed shallowly into deeply worked, stone-free soil, since forked or stunted roots result from compacted ground; keep the seedbed evenly moist through slow germination and thin seedlings to a few inches apart. This long-standing English heirloom is prized for roots that are smooth-skinned, nearly coreless, and unusually tender for a full-season parsnip, with good field tolerance to canker. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert starch to sugar and give the roots their signature sweet, nutty flavor.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed once soil is workable in spring; mark rows clearly since parsnip emergence is slow and easy to mistake for weeds.

directions: Direct sow shallowly into loose, deeply dug soil free of rocks and clods so the long roots can develop without forking, and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding. Lancer is valued by market gardeners for its smooth white skin, uniform wedge shape, and strong resistance to canker, a common fungal problem that disfigures many older parsnip varieties. Allow roots to remain in the ground after the first fall frosts to develop their full sweetness before digging for storage or immediate use.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors and transplant carefully; give this giant type much more room than standard kohlrabi so the stem can bulk up over a long season.

directions: Sow into fertile, well-drained soil with wide spacing, since Superschmelz — German for super melter — is bred to swell to eight or ten pounds while staying crisp and tender rather than turning woody like most oversized kohlrabi. Keep watering consistent through the growing season to avoid splitting the enlarging stem, and side-dress with compost as the bulb sizes up. Harvest young for a milder, thinner-skinned bite, or let it grow to full giant size for slicing, roasting, or long winter storage.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into deep, fertile, evenly moist soil, since celeriac's long development window punishes any lapse in watering with cracked or hollow roots. Brilliant is grown for its notably smooth-skinned, low-knobbed globes, which peel far more cleanly than older, rougher celeriac types while keeping the same concentrated celery flavor. Remove side shoots and surface roots from the developing globe through the season to channel growth into the main root, and harvest in fall for a dense, long-storing crop that holds well in a root cellar.
